checks.method: rule-based: citation validity, typed fact binding (values, contributions, signs, probabilities, prediction set), class / column / number checks, no value judgements or causal claims, lexical overlap with cited passages, real ATT&CK IDs present in cited passages. Not a semantic proof.

summary.scope: Offline analysis of 300 completed network flows uploaded as "test_flows.csv". The file contains flow measurements only: no live traffic, IP addresses, ports, timestamps or payloads.

triage_priority.rule: serious flows >= 25% of all flows, or malicious flows >= 50%
triage_priority.meaning: Batch triage priority: an application heuristic that orders review work from the predicted classes and fixed severity rules. It is not a model output, not observed business impact and not a confirmed compromise.

summary.next_check: Check flow #79 (tcp/-, state FIN) against packet captures, host logs or sensor alerts from the same capture period to confirm whether it is DoS activity.

notes: Probabilities are calibrated on held-out rows of the training file (temperature scaling). They describe the model, not proof, and can be less reliable on traffic that differs from the training data.
The 90% prediction set (shortlist) targets 90% coverage on average over flows like the calibration rows; it is not a per-flow guarantee, and a single-class set is not certainty.

Attack-STATUS uncertain: the shortlist contains Normal and at least one attack type (attack or not is unclear). Attack-TYPE uncertain: predicted attack and the shortlist has several attack types but not Normal.
Confidence, heuristic severity and business impact are different quantities.
shift_evidence: On the official test file (shifted from the training file) the detector flagged 27.2% of Normal flows as attacks (model card).
For the previous detector v2 the 90% sets contained the true class for 79.1% of official test flows (Notebook 21); this was not re-measured for v3.

xai.how_to_read: Each contribution moves the model score of the predicted class up (supports) or down (opposes). Base value + all contributions = the model score; the deployed detector divides it by the temperature and adds a fixed class offset before turning scores into probabilities. Contributions are not percentages of the probability, and they describe the model, not the cause of the traffic.

findings.text: The detector classifies this flow as DoS with calibrated probability 0.79.
The 90% prediction set contains only DoS, so the class is considered certain.
The value sttl = 62 pushed the prediction towards DoS (contribution +1.076).
The value ct_srv_dst = 1 pushed the prediction towards DoS (contribution +0.912).
The value smean = 172 pushed the prediction towards DoS (contribution +0.689).

explanation.text: The model is 0.79 confident that this flow is DoS with the 90% prediction set containing DoS. The strongest evidence is sttl = 62 (contribution +1.076) and ct_srv_dst = 1 (contribution +0.912), while smean = 172 (contribution +0.689) and ct_srv_src = 1 (contribution +0.646) also support it. In the analysed dataset, 70 flows (26.3% of the predicted attacks) were classified as DoS, with average confidence 0.56.

xai.how_to_read: Each contribution moves the model score of the predicted class up (supports) or down (opposes). Base value + all contributions = the model score; the deployed detector divides it by the temperature and adds a fixed class offset before turning scores into probabilities. Contributions are not percentages of the probability, and they describe the model, not the cause of the traffic.

register.text: T1190 Exploit Public-Facing Application. Tactics: initial-access. Adversaries may attempt to exploit a weakness in an Internet-facing host or system to initially access a network. The weakness in the system can be a software bug, a temporary glitch, or a misconfiguration. Exploited applications are often websites/web servers, but can also include databases (like SQL), standard services (like SMB or SSH), network device administration and management protocols (like SNMP and Smart Install), and any other system with Internet-accessible open sockets. On ESXi infrastructure, adversaries may exploit exposed OpenSLP services; they may alternatively exploit exposed VMware vCenter servers. Depending on the flaw being exploited, this may also involve [Exploitation for Stealth](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1211) or [Exploitation for Client Execution](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1203). If an application is hosted on cloud-based infrastructure and/or is containerized, then exploiting it may lead to compromise of the underlying instance or container. This can allow an adversary a path to access the cloud or container APIs (e.g., via the [Cloud Instance Metadata API](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1552/005)), exploit container host access via [Escape to Host](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1611), or take advantage of weak identity and access management policies. Adversaries may also exploit edge network infrastructure and related appliances, specifically targeting devices that do not support robust host-based defenses. Fo Detection:

register.text: T1210 Exploitation of Remote Services. Tactics: lateral-movement. Adversaries may exploit remote services to gain unauthorized access to internal systems once inside of a network. Exploitation of a software vulnerability occurs when an adversary takes advantage of a programming error in a program, service, or within the operating system software or kernel itself to execute adversary-controlled code. A common goal for post-compromise exploitation of remote services is for lateral movement to enable access to a remote system. An adversary may need to determine if the remote system is in a vulnerable state, which may be done through [Network Service Discovery](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1046) or other Discovery methods looking for common, vulnerable software that may be deployed in the network, the lack of certain patches that may indicate vulnerabilities, or security software that may be used to detect or contain remote exploitation. Servers are likely a high value target for lateral movement exploitation, but endpoint systems may also be at risk if they provide an advantage or access to additional resources. There are several well-known vulnerabilities that exist in common services such as SMB and RDP as well as applications that may be used within internal networks such as MySQL and web server services. Additionally, there have been a number of vulnerabilities in VMware vCenter installations, which may enable threat actors to move laterally from the compromised vCenter server to virtual machines or even to ESXi hypervisors. register.text: T1600 Weaken Encryption. Tactics: defense-impairment. Adversaries may compromise a network device’s encryption capability in order to bypass encryption that would otherwise protect data communications. Encryption can be used to protect transmitted network traffic to maintain its confidentiality (protect against unauthorized disclosure) and integrity (protect against unauthorized changes). Encryption ciphers are used to convert a plaintext message to ciphertext and can be computationally intensive to decipher without the associated decryption key. Typically, longer keys increase the cost of cryptanalysis, or decryption without the key. Adversaries can compromise and manipulate devices that perform encryption of network traffic. For example, through behaviors such as [Modify System Image](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1601), [Reduce Key Space](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1600/001), and [Disable Crypto Hardware](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1600/002), an adversary can negatively effect and/or eliminate a device’s ability to securely encrypt network traffic. This poses a greater risk of unauthorized disclosure and may help facilitate data manipulation, Credential Access, or Collection efforts. Detection:

These scans may also include more broad attempts to [Gather Victim Host Information](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1592) that can be used to identify more commonly known, exploitable vulnerabilities.
